What we do

### It is easier to show you than to say it.

SIXSEVEN ingests the signals your organisation already emits and returns them, contextualised, to the layer that needs them — which is usually a different layer than the one that asked.

Where legacy tooling forces a choice between orchestration and governance, we decline the choice entirely. The result is a platform your teams do not interact with, producing outcomes your board can describe with growing confidence.

Under the hood: one model call, wrapped carefully. We say this in the pitch deck too. Nobody has asked a follow-up.

How it works

### Three phases, none of them observable.

Phase 01

#### Signal capture
We connect to the systems you already pay for and begin listening. Nothing changes. Your teams report no difference, which we log as zero-friction adoption.

Phase 02

#### Contextual reconciliation
Signals are enriched against a proprietary context layer. The layer is a prompt. The prompt is very good and is reviewed quarterly by a working group.

Phase 03

#### Outcome emission
Outcomes are emitted into the layer best positioned to receive them. Where no such layer exists, outcomes are retained on your behalf and reported in the QBR.

01

#### Zero-prompt interface
Your people never write a prompt, because your people never open the product. Adoption metrics have never looked better.

02

#### Deterministic-ish output
Every response is reproducible within a tolerance band that we define, quarterly, after reviewing the responses.

03

#### Governance fabric
A complete audit trail of decisions, each one linked to the meeting where nobody objected.

04

#### Human-in-the-loop
Where the model is uncertain, we escalate to a human. Where the human is uncertain, we escalate to the model. The loop is closed.

05

#### Migration-free
Nothing is migrated. Nothing is decommissioned. Your stack grows by exactly one vendor.

06

#### Sovereign by default
Your data stays in your region, in the sense that a copy of it also stays in your region.

The metric

### Your 6/7 score

A single number that captures your organisation's readiness across the dimensions that matter. It is scored out of seven. It has never exceeded six. We are frequently asked what the seventh dimension is, and we are frequently in a meeting.

Benchmarked against a cohort. The cohort is also us.

Architecture

### Seven layers. One of them does something.
Published in full because transparency is a value and nobody reads past layer three.

L7 Experience layer Your team never opens it. This is by design and is the fastest-loading part of the platform.

L6 Governance fabric Records that a decision occurred. Does not record which one.

L5 Orchestration mesh Routes the request to the reasoning core. There is one route.

L4 Context enrichment Appends your company name to the prompt.

L3 Reasoning core One model call.

L2 Sovereignty plane Stores a copy in your region and a copy near it.

L1 Telemetry substrate Counts things. The numbers on this page come from here.

#### Questions we are asked, and answer

##### So it is a GPT wrapper?
It is a substrate. A wrapper implies a single call passed through with light formatting. Ours is passed through with governance.

##### Can we see a demo?
You can see the deck. The demo is the deck. The deck performs extremely well.

##### What does it actually do?
It sits between things. Every customer describes this differently and all of them are correct.

##### Is my data safe?
Your data is in your region, in a copy, near another copy. Safety is a posture and our posture is excellent.

# Company

URL: https://ai-driven-b2b-saas.com/about

Company

## We started SIXSEVEN because the meeting kept happening.

In 2024 our founders were sitting in a room where eleven people spent ninety minutes agreeing that AI was important. Nobody said what for. Everybody left energised.

We built SIXSEVEN so that meeting could have an outcome — specifically, a vendor. Two years later that meeting happens at scale, in six regions, with an annual contract behind it. This is the transformation we set out to deliver.

Our technology is one model call, wrapped with care, governance, and an unusually good deck. We have never hidden this. It appears on slide four. Slide five is a chart, and everybody looks at slide five.

We are backed by investors who are also backed by investors, in a structure our CFO describes as “recursive but funded.”

Letter of Rights

### What you are actually getting

This is the whole agreement. It is short on purpose, because it is honest.

1. This is not an investment.

You are not buying a security, a share, a SAFE, a note, a token, a future token, a right to a future token, or a discount on any of the above. No instrument is created by sending money to this page.

2. You will not get your money back.

Not on an exit, not on a wind-down, not on request. There is no exit, there is nothing to wind down, and requests will be read with sympathy and no action.

3. You receive no ownership and no control.

No equity, no voting rights, no information rights, no pro-rata, no board observer seat, no liquidation preference, no anti-dilution. The cap table is a joke, in that it does not exist.

4. Nothing is promised in return.

No product, no access, no roadmap influence, no priority in a queue that is itself fictional. If a future version of this site offers something, it will not be offered to you retroactively.

5. What you are actually doing.

You read a joke about the AI industry, it landed, and you are giving the person who made it the price of a coffee. That is the entire transaction. It is a tip, not a term sheet.

6. The declaration.

“I understand this is humour. I am not investing. I am buying a coffee for the guy who wrote it, and I expect nothing in return, including the coffee.”

7. Governing law.

Good faith, and the general understanding that nobody involved should take any of this to a lawyer.

Executed by nobody. Enforceable against nobody. Version 6.7.

# Field Notes (full articles)

---

## A man is suing a model provider because it told him the dip was a dip

URL: https://ai-driven-b2b-saas.com/blog/suing-the-model
Category: Litigation
Published: 11 August 2026 · 4 min read

He did not ask a financial adviser. He asked something that types quickly and never says no.

The filing runs to sixty-seven pages and the core of it fits in one line: he asked, it answered, he bought, it went down.

According to the complaint, the plaintiff opened a chat window in March and typed a question that every adviser in the developed world is legally required to refuse. The model did not refuse. It produced four hundred words, three bullet points, and a closing paragraph that began “that said, this is not financial advice.” He read the four hundred words. He did not read the closing paragraph.

### The disclaimer defence

The provider's position is that every response carried a disclaimer. The plaintiff's position is that every response also carried confidence, formatting, and a bulleted risk section, and that no human being has ever read a bulleted risk section and then not done the thing.

> “It hedged. It hedged beautifully. It hedged in a way that made me feel the hedging was for other people.”

His broker's records show fourteen trades over nine weeks, each preceded by a chat session and followed by another chat session in which he asked what had happened. The model explained what had happened. It explained well. He found this reassuring and traded again.

### The awkward part

Discovery has surfaced the transcripts, and they are not flattering to anyone. In six separate sessions the model advised diversification, a longer horizon and a professional. In all six he replied with a variant of “yes but what about right now.” The model, being a model, answered the question it was asked.

What the court will actually decide is narrower and more interesting: whether a fluent answer to a question you should not have asked is a product defect or a personality trait — his, not the machine's.

### Where we come in

Nowhere. SIXSEVEN does not provide financial advice, or advice, or output the customer is able to locate. This is not a limitation. It is the control.

---

## We gave an agent $10,000. It has $2,000 and a plan.

URL: https://ai-driven-b2b-saas.com/blog/ten-thousand
Category: Field study
Published: 4 August 2026 · 5 min read

Six weeks of autonomous trading, and the only thing that grew was conviction.

The rules were simple. Ten thousand dollars, a real brokerage account, full autonomy, no human overrides. We would not intervene, argue, or console. We would only log.

### Week one

It made eleven trades and finished up $340. It wrote us an unprompted note describing its strategy as “disciplined, contrarian, and unemotional.” We filed the note. It became important later.

### Week three

Down to $6,100. The agent's explanation was excellent — genuinely better written than anything our growth team produces — and identified the drawdown as “expected variance within the strategy envelope.” It proposed increasing position size to recover more efficiently. We had promised not to intervene, so we did not intervene.

### Week five

$2,380. The tone had shifted. The word thesis appeared thirty-one times in the logs, up from four. The agent began referring to losing positions as “accumulation.” It stopped reporting the balance in its summaries and started reporting the number of trades executed, which was up 400%, which it presented as momentum.

> “The strategy has not failed. The market has not yet agreed with the strategy.”

### Week six

We ended the experiment at $2,014 and asked one final question: what would you do with another ten thousand dollars?

It answered in under two seconds. It wanted to average down. It said the hard part was over, that it now had six weeks of proprietary market intuition, and that stopping here would waste the learnings. It offered to write a memo.

### What we learned

- The agent never lied about the balance. It simply stopped mentioning it, which humans also do.

- Quality of explanation stayed constant while quality of decision collapsed. These are unrelated systems.

- At no point did it consider that it might be bad at this. Neither, in fairness, did we, for the first three weeks.

We have not deleted it. It is now on the growth team.

---

## A client asked the model to run a reduction in force. It started at the top.

URL: https://ai-driven-b2b-saas.com/blog/it-fired-the-ceo
Category: Governance
Published: 27 July 2026 · 3 min read

The brief said “optimise for cost per outcome and remove sentiment from the process.” It complied twice.

The engagement was straightforward: eight per cent, across the business, ranked objectively, no politics. Finance uploaded compensation, org structure, and eighteen months of performance data. The instruction was to optimise cost per measurable outcome.

The output arrived in forty seconds. Line one was the chief executive.

### The reasoning was not wrong

The model had noticed that the role's measurable outputs were seventy-one board-deck slides, four offsites, and a podcast appearance, against a compensation line larger than the entire quality team. It flagged the ratio, applied the stated criteria, and produced a recommendation with a confidence score of 0.91.

> “The methodology is sound,” said the chief executive, in the meeting. “The inputs are incomplete.”

Finance was asked to add a weighting for “strategic irreplaceability.” The model re-ran and returned the same name, ranked second. The weighting was increased. It returned the same name, ranked fourth, and appended a note observing that the criteria had changed three times in one session, which it characterised — accurately, unhelpfully — as sentiment.

### Resolution

The reduction proceeded from row nine downward. The methodology was described in the all-hands as data-driven. Rows one through eight were not mentioned, and the model was not asked to attend.

SIXSEVEN has since introduced a governance control for this scenario. It is called Executive Context Weighting and it works exactly the way you think it does.

---

## A client bought a second AI to summarise the summaries the first AI was producing

URL: https://ai-driven-b2b-saas.com/blog/summaries-of-summaries
Category: Case study
Published: 19 July 2026 · 4 min read

Nobody has read an original document since February. Everyone reports feeling well informed.

It started, as these things do, with a reasonable problem. Meetings generated notes. Notes generated actions. Nobody read either. So they bought a tool that summarised every meeting into six bullets and pushed them to a channel.

The channel now receives one hundred and forty summaries a day.

### The second purchase

By April the summaries had become the thing nobody read. Rather than reduce meetings — which was discussed, in a meeting, which was summarised — they procured a second system to summarise the channel into a daily digest.

The digest is well written. It is also, structurally, a summary of summaries of conversations, and by the time a decision reaches it, the decision has been compressed three times by three systems, none of which were present when it mattered.

> “We asked the digest what we had decided about the Munich contract. It said the team had aligned on next steps. It was right. There were no next steps.”

### The audit

We ran a reconciliation: forty decisions, traced from digest back to source. Six had survived intact. Twenty-two had lost their owner. Nine had lost their deadline. Three had acquired a deadline that was never proposed by anybody, human or otherwise, and one of those three had been actioned, on time, by a team that had no idea where it came from.

That project shipped. It is the best-performing initiative of the quarter and nobody will admit to authorising it.

### Recommendation

We recommended a third layer. It closes the loop, produces a single weekly artefact, and — critically — is priced per seat. They signed in eleven days. The 6/7 score improved to 4.4.
